hints: Look closely at the three terms and ask yourself if they are three separate ideas or three linked parts of the same story in a narrow xylem tube.
Remember why water molecules stick to each other so strongly, and what that stickiness allows them to do when pulled from the top by transpiration.
walkthrough:
**Start with the property of water**

Think about water molecules in the xylem. They are polar and form hydrogen bonds with each other. This is the foundation for everything else.

Key idea: hydrogen bonding is the chemical cause.

**Link hydrogen bonding to cohesion**

Because of those hydrogen bonds, one water molecule pulls strongly on the next. We call this water-to-water attraction cohesion. It lets water form an unbroken column that can be pulled up as one unit.

So: hydrogen bonding causes cohesion, and cohesion transmits the transpiration pull.

**Add capillary action**

Xylem vessels are very narrow, hollow tubes. Water also sticks to the walls (adhesion) and to itself (cohesion), so it can rise a little by capillary action. This helps movement, especially in narrow vessels, alongside the main transpiration pull.

Conclusion: all three, 1, 2 and 3, play a role, so the answer is A.

options.A: Correct and reassuring. Hydrogen bonding causes cohesion, which holds the water column together, and both help capillary rise in narrow xylem vessels.
options.B: Close but incomplete. It correctly includes 1 and 2, but misses that hydrogen bonding in 3 is the underlying cause of cohesion.
options.C: Close but incomplete. It correctly includes 1 and 3, but misses that cohesion in 2 is essential to pull the whole water column up.
options.D: Too narrow. Hydrogen bonding alone is true, but on its own it ignores its effects, which are cohesion and capillary action.
